column1: # Engine-parity regression classes, from the boru differential-probe report
# against @tabnas/parser + @tabnas/jsonic (fixed upstream in parser 0.8.0 /
# jsonic 0.6.0). These pin how each class manifests through aontu's OWN
# semantics — where the engine's old defects variously fabricated list
# elements, destroyed characters, or silently swallowed separators, aontu
# must instead give either a clean value or a clean aontu error.
# Columns: name<TAB>mode<TAB>src<TAB>expect ; mode: canon|gen|err
# Base-prefixed run with a dot continuation: lexes as TEXT whole (engine
# adjudication), and a bare dotted word in aontu is a path REFERENCE — so
# these resolve like any other unresolvable ref: a clean no_path/negative
# error, identical to a:[zz.qq]. The old TS engine fabricated elements here
# ([0xFF.5] parsed as [[],"xFF.5"]) and destroyed the leading character.
prefix-dot-ref-err
prefix-dot-ref-err2
prefix-dot-ref-neg
prefix-dot-ref-same
# Separator at a run edge: not a number (engine adjudication: separators
# only between digits). The old Go engine parsed +_1 as the NUMBER 1,
# silently changing user data; 1_ as 1.
sep-edge-str
sep-edge-list
# Unary + on a non-number is aontu's expr semantics (the operator yields
# its operand), NOT character corruption: +x behaves identically.
sep-edge-unary
unary-plus-word
unary-plus-num
# Protected baselines: interior separators and base-prefixed literals.
baseline-sep
baseline-hex
baseline-hex-list
# Integer-like keys: generated JSON enumerates them ascending (a JS/plain
# representation semantic on both ports; source order is not preserved in
# gen output).
intkey-order
# MAP KEY ORDER IS LEXICOGRAPHIC, IN GENERATED JSON AS WELL AS CANON.
# The intkey-order row above pins nothing: `gen` decodes before comparing,
# so it is order-blind in BOTH runners, and its example {2:9,1:8} is one
# where numeric and lexicographic order coincide. These rows use `gens`,
# which compares the serialised bytes, and keys where the two orders differ.
# TypeScript emitted integer-like keys in ascending NUMERIC order, ahead of
# every other key -- not a design rule but ECMAScript's own property order
# (OrdinaryOwnPropertyKeys hoists canonical array indices, ascending), which
# silently discarded the lexicographic sort BagVal.gen had already done.
# TS's own CANON was lexicographic throughout, so the port contradicted
# itself; the canon rows below pin the half that was already right.
# The 2^32 row is the one that proves the cause: only indices up to 2^32-2
# are hoisted, so 4294967296 stays behind while 5 and 4294967295 jump ahead
# of it. No ordering rule anyone would design produces that.
intkey-order-multidigit
intkey-order-punct
intkey-order-mixed-alpha
intkey-order-index-limit
intkey-order-nested
intkey-order-in-list
intkey-order-canon
intkey-order-canon-punct
intkey-order-canon-commute-a
intkey-order-canon-commute-b
